kemeny1979.title: The Need for Change: The Legacy of TMI — Report of the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island
kemeny1979.author: John G. Kemeny, Chairman; President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island
kemeny1979.quote: At 4:00 a.m. on March 28, 1979, a serious accident occurred at the Three Mile Island 2 nuclear power plant near Middletown, Pennsylvania. ... The PORV indicator light in the control room showed only that the signal had been sent to close the PORV rather than the fact that the PORV remained open. ... The PORV should have closed 13 seconds into the accident, when pressure dropped to 2,205 psi. It did not. A light on the control room panel indicated that the electric power that opened the PORV had gone off, leading the operators to assume the valve had shut. But the PORV was stuck open, and would remain open for 2 hours and 22 minutes ... In the first 100 minutes of the accident, some 32,000 gallons -- over one-third of the entire capacity of the reactor coolant system -- would escape through the PORV ... In spite of this, this control room might be adequate for the normal operation of nuclear power plants. However, it is seriously deficient under accident conditions. During the first few minutes of the accident, more than 100 alarms went off, and there was no system for suppressing the unimportant signals so that operators could concentrate on the significant alarms. ... The computer printer registering alarms was running more than 2-k hours behind the events and at one point jammed, thereby losing valuable information. ... Later Faust would recall for the Commission his reaction to the incessant alarms: "I would have liked to have thrown away the alarm panel. It wasn't giving us any useful information." ... A shift supervisor testified that there had never been less than 52 alarms lit in the control room. ... The direct financial cost of the accident is enormous. Our best estimate puts it in a range of $1 to $2 billion, even if TMI-2 can be put back into operation.
kemeny1979.note: Read from the PDF hosted by Dickinson College's TMI archive (188.pdf, 178pp). Page 1 is a scanned cover image; the body pages carry no image and render from an embedded Courier New subset, i.e. the body is an OCR text layer, not the original scan. One consequence is visible in Commission Finding B.8.b.iv, where the printer's lag renders as "2-k hours" both in pdftotext and in a 500-dpi pdftoppm render of the page: the fraction glyph is corrupted in the document itself and is not recoverable from it. See 'unverified'. Cover title confirmed from the page-1 scan. Passages sit in the Preface ('The Accident'), the Overview, Commission Findings A.3 and B.8.b, Commission Findings on utility management, and 'Account of the Accident'; the A.3 numbering is confirmed by the cross-reference '(See finding A.3.)' at Findings B.1.f. This volume carries no date of its own; the October 1979 date used on card p2c08-c3 comes from the Commission's companion volumes, whose title page reads 'October 1979 / Washington, D.C.'

tmitaskforce1979.title: Reports of the Technical Assessment Task Force, Volume I: Technical Staff Analysis Reports Summary / Summary Sequence of Events
tmitaskforce1979.author: Technical Assessment Task Force (Leonard Jaffe, Head), President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island
tmitaskforce1979.quote: A few seconds before 4:00:37 a.m. on March 28, 1979, the condensate polisher outlet valves shut causing the condensate booster pumps to trip due to low suction pressure which caused the main feedwater pumps to trip from low suction pressure at 4:00:37. ... The valve position light on the control panel indicated that the valve was closed but it only indicates electrical power applied to an actuation solenoid in the valve and not valve position. ... The operators were aware that the PORV had lifted but thought the valve had closed because the valve position indicator light was extinguished. This indicator only indicated that power was applied to the pilot solenoid for the PORV and did not indicate valve stem position. ... 06:22:37(02:22:00) The PORV block valve was shut. ... Note: Over 100 alarms occurred during the first few minutes of the accident. ... There are more than 1,500 alarms in the plant with most of them being annunciated in the control room. Alarms are not arranged in the control room in a logical fashion.
tmitaskforce1979.note: Stock Number 052-003-00728-2, October 1979, Washington, D.C. Read from 195.pdf in Dickinson College's TMI archive. As with 188.pdf, page 1 is a scanned cover image and the body is an OCR text layer in an embedded Courier New subset, not a scan; text extracted with pdftotext. Title page reads 'REPORTS OF THE TECHNICAL ASSESSMENT TASK FORCE ... VOLUME I / October 1979 / Washington, D.C.' Independently corroborates the Kemeny volume on the solenoid wiring, the 4:00:37 a.m. initiating event and the 2h22m valve-open interval.

nrckm0001s1.title: Three Mile Island Accident of 1979 Knowledge Management Digest: Recovery and Cleanup (NUREG/KM-0001, Supplement 1)
nrckm0001s1.author: US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Office of Nuclear Regulatory Research
nrckm0001s1.quote: This supplement chronicles those activities, which began a week following the accident, and ended with the completion of disposal of accident-generated water, and entry into post-defueling monitored storage in 1993. ... This knowledge management volume ends with the licensing of the PDMS configuration and the issuance of the PDMS technical specifications at the end of 1993.
nrckm0001s1.note: Read from the govinfo mirror; nrc.gov serves 403 to non-browser clients. Cover date June 2016. Cleanup therefore ran from April 1979 to the end of 1993 — fourteen years.
supports: cleanup ran another fourteen years, ending in 1993

unverified: EEMUA Publication 191 (1999) setting a steady-state target of roughly one alarm per operator per ten minutes — the standard is paywalled and was not opened, so no alarm-rate benchmark appears in the prose.
The claim that no new US nuclear plant construction start followed for about three decades — not confirmed against a primary source and therefore not used.

Whether the shift supervisor who testified to 'never less than 52 alarms' was William Zewe, the supervisor on duty on 28 March 1979. The Commission finding says only 'A shift supervisor', so no name is attached to it in the prose or on a card.
The often-quoted $973 million total cleanup cost. The only cost figure used is the Commission's own $1 to $2 billion direct-cost estimate.

How far behind the alarm printer was running. Commission Finding B.8.b.iv says 'more than 2-k hours behind the events' in the only text of the report that could be opened, where '2-k' is a corrupted fraction; no second source could be reached to resolve it (nrc.gov and threemileisland.org 403 non-browser clients, HathiTrust 403s, the session's web-search budget was spent). The figure is therefore out of the prose, which now claims only what the finding says without the number: the printer ran behind the events and jammed.
